newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore corporate tax seen falling - W.I. Carr.
newsitem.headline: Singapore corporate tax seen falling - W.I. Carr.

text.p: Singapore is likely to use fiscal measures such as a corporate tax cut to boost its flagging economy rather than relying on currency weakness, W.I. Carr said on Thursday.

While Singapore's non-oil domestic export growth is likely to remain weak in the first half of this year, the authorities will not use the exchange rate to stimulate exports, W.I. Carr said in a research note.
"Although the appreciation of the Singapore dollar has slowed somewhat...there is no denying the fact Singapore's exchange rate policy is guided by the objective of controlling inflation," it said.
A strong currency would also help Singapore concentrate on exports of capital rather than goods and services, it said.

W.I. Carr said the Singapore dollar's recent weakness against the U.S. dollar was temporary and caused by an abnormal strengthening of the U.S. dollar, weak sentiment due to Singapore's poor February exports and strained bilateral ties with Malaysia.
It said the Singapore dollar was likely to return to its appreciating trend in the second quarter and could touch 1.38 to the U.S. dollar by year end, from around 1.43-1.44 now.
The monetary tightening effected through a stronger currency coupled with a pick-up in loan demand in the second half would mean higher interest rates later in the year.

"Now that currency weakening is ruled out as a measure to stimulate the economy, the authorities are expected to use fiscal pump-priming," it said, adding that the most likely measure was a corporate tax cut in the next budget.
The corporate tax rate, currently 26 percent, could be lowered by between one and three percentage points in the fiscal 1997 budget, expected to be announced by August.
A lower tax rate would boost the corporate sector and increase its attractiveness to foreign investors.
It would also be in line with Singapore's long-term goal of shifting to consumption-based taxes, which it sees as fairer than income-based taxes.

"Although a three percent cut in corporate tax rate appears to conflict the government's objective of building up fiscal reserves, the final impact may be negligible on the fiscal surplus," the W.I. Carr report said.
